newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-US industrial output seen up mildy in Aug.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-US industrial output seen up mildy in Aug.

text.p: Industrial production data due on Tuesday are likely to show the U.S. manufacturing sector grew mildly in August, hinting output remains firm but weaker than in the second quarter, analysts said.
"The report should show some decent gains in industrial production. Not robust, but solid gains," said Josh Feinman, global markets economist at BT Securities Inc.
In a Reuters survey, economists expect August industrial production to rise 0.4 percent against a 0.1-percent increase in July.
The Federal Reserve will issue the industrial output and capacity utilization report on Tuesday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Average forecasts put capacity utilization at 83.3 percent in August, up very slightly from the 83.2 percent registered the previous month.
Analysts said most of the expected gains in the manufacturing sector stem from a mild, broad-based inventory re-building that started in late July.
"The industrial sector is catching up to where the economy is because people have stopped cutting their inventories," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.

However, analysts said auto output, seen by many as a benchmark in the sector, is likely to buck the trend and show a weaker performance in August since those firms had started to re-build their inventories earlier.
"The auto makers were building inventories in June and July and that lifted production higher than it would've been otherwise," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
"In August they stopped to build up ... So we're likely to see very small overall gains (in industrial production)," Low added.
If the data come in as expected, analysts said the figures will confirm the market's general belief that the economy in general is slowing from the heady growth levels seen earlier in the year.

Second quarter Gross Domestic Product posted a 4.8-percent growth pace, the highest since the 4.9 percent registered in the second quarter of 1994. A slowing economy, pundits added, is also likely to keep inflation in check.
"We ought to see very small gains ... and again this is the kind of growth that is prefectly sustainable without inflation," Low added.
BT's Feinman agreed, saying, "The manufacturing sector is doing fine, but not overheating."

For the domestic money market, analysts said the data will have little effect on trading. "The IP numbers are likely to have a muted impact on the (money) market," said a trader at a U.S. bank. "Unless we see a huge surprise, we expect the market to mostly shrug off the data," he added.
